title: VlogReward: Learning Multi-Dimensional Evaluation for Vlog Editing
one_liner: Turn vlog editing quality into six explicit scoring dimensions, then train a reward model that can rank edits, explain what failed, and drive iterative improvement with a stronger preference-learning signal.
lead: Automated vlog editing is difficult because an edit is not judged by one property. A good edit must preserve the creator's concept, maintain story consistency across shots, choose clips that support narration, keep pacing under control, and use camera material in a visually coherent way. If a model receives only one coarse score, it cannot tell which of those requirements failed, so its feedback is weak and its training signal is noisy. VlogReward addresses that problem by building a six-part evaluation framework, collecting a large dataset of edited vlogs, and training a reward model that outputs both dimension-level scores and textual feedback. The technical core is a modified Group Relative Policy Optimization setup that adds adjustable comparisons across groups of examples, so the reward model learns not only which edit is better inside a local batch but also how quality changes across a broader range of edit quality levels, because those extra comparisons tell the model how far apart weak, medium, and strong edits are.

problem.h2: Why vlog editing is hard to score automatically
paras: A vlog edit is a structured plan over footage, audio, and narrative intent. The system must decide which clips to keep, how long they should stay on screen, where transitions should occur, and whether the sequence supports the creator's stated story. That makes evaluation fundamentally multi-criteria. An edit can be visually attractive yet break the story, or it can preserve the story but feel dull because pacing is poor.

Existing reward models and multimodal judges often compress all of that into one overall preference label. That is a weak signal because two edits with the same overall score may fail for completely different reasons. A model trained on such labels may learn shallow correlations, such as preferring faster cuts or brighter footage, without understanding whether the edit actually improved narration, consistency, or concept execution, because the label never identifies which editing dimension caused the preference.

The paper's first move is to define the criteria explicitly. The second move is to make the training signal sensitive to direction, meaning whether one candidate is slightly better, clearly better, or better on a specific dimension, because refinement needs to know what type of improvement happened and how large it was.

callout.html: Replace one coarse overall idea of edit quality with a six-dimensional reward model that can rank, diagnose, and guide improvement of vlog edits.

steps.text: Specify six dimensions that together capture whether a vlog edit is coherent, visually effective, and aligned with the creator's story.
Build a large dataset of vlog edits and a benchmark so the reward model sees broad variation in quality and style.
Feed the model edit plans and associated multimodal evidence so it can predict per-dimension scores and feedback.
Add adjustable inter-group comparison rewards so the learner can tell not only which edit wins locally, but also how far apart quality levels are across groups.
Use the model's score breakdown and textual feedback to revise weak dimensions in the next editing round.

paras: The paper changes the reward signal used for automated vlog editing. Instead of asking a model for one overall judgment, it turns editing quality into a structured multi-dimensional supervision problem and then strengthens the preference-learning objective used to train that judge.
object.object: the reward model and its training signal for vlog edit evaluation

hidden.name: directional edit quality across dimensions
paras: The key quantity is not just whether Edit A beats Edit B. The useful quantity is how an edit is improving or degrading along each editing dimension. If one revision improves pacing but breaks narration, the system should not collapse those changes into an opaque net score because the next editing step needs that diagnostic detail.

The paper argues that standard GRPO suffers from direction blindness, meaning the optimization signal can say that one item is preferred within a comparison group without clearly representing the broader ordering across groups of different quality levels. The adjustable inter-group reward fixes that by supplying additional comparisons that make the relative direction of improvement more explicit. That matters because a reward model trained on richer order information can separate mediocre edits from truly strong ones and can attach feedback to the dimensions responsible for the gap.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the dimension-level and cross-group signals that reveal where quality is changing and which edit revision should come next.

reads.html: The model needs to know which parts of the edit improved, which parts got worse, and how strong that change was.
The reward learner should encode fine-grained multidimensional quality and stable preference direction across local and inter-group comparisons.

paras: The six-dimensional rubric matters because editing quality is not a single hidden property that can be inferred reliably from surface polish. Each dimension corresponds to a different decision pattern. Creativity concerns whether the edit makes purposeful, engaging choices. Consistency checks whether the sequence preserves topic and visual continuity. Concept Design asks whether the edit expresses the intended story or theme. Cinematography evaluates shot quality and visual composition. Narration checks whether the edit supports spoken or implied storytelling. Pacing evaluates whether timing and cut rhythm help comprehension instead of hurting it, because cuts that arrive too early or too late break the flow of information the viewer needs. Making those factors explicit gives the reward model a stable target.

The training objective matters for a different reason. In preference learning, a model can perform adequately on easy within-group comparisons yet still fail to build a useful global quality ordering. That is a problem for refinement because edit revision is inherently sequential: the system must know whether a candidate is marginally better or substantially better, and why. Inter-group comparison rewards provide supervision across broader quality ranges, so the reward model learns a more calibrated ranking function. The textual feedback head then converts that ranking signal into edit advice by tying poor scores to specific dimensions.

The benchmark and dataset matter because subjective tasks need enough coverage to prevent the reward model from overfitting one creator style. Large-scale examples across diverse vlogs force the model to learn the underlying editing criteria rather than memorizing a narrow aesthetic pattern.

math.h2: A simple way to express the reward
math.words: The total training reward combines dimension-level scoring with both within-group and cross-group preference comparisons so the model learns a calibrated ranking signal.
math.equation: R = sum_d w_d * s_d + alpha * R_intra + beta * R_inter
symbols: total reward signal used to train the evaluator
predicted score on dimension d such as pacing or narration
relative preference reward for comparisons within a local group of candidates
relative preference reward for comparisons across different quality groups
strength of the within-group comparison term
strength of the inter-group comparison term

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an edit gets dimension scores: creativity 0.6, consistency 0.8, concept 0.7, cinematography 0.9, narration 0.4, pacing 0.3.
If each dimension weight is 1, the dimension subtotal is 3.7.
Inside its local group, the edit beats most neighbors, so R_intra = 0.5.
Across broader quality groups, it still ranks below strong edits because narration and pacing are weak, so R_inter = -0.4.
With alpha = 1 and beta = 2, total reward is 3.7 + 0.5 + 2 * (-0.4) = 3.4.
The result says the edit is decent overall but still below the stronger tier, and the score profile shows narration and pacing as the main revision targets.

math.note: The exact loss in the paper is more detailed, but this form captures the main idea: edit quality should be dimension-aware and globally ordered, not only locally ranked.

charts.title: Coarse multimodal judge
charts.note: A one-score judge can rank obvious winners, but it gives weak guidance for iterative editing because it does not separate the reasons an edit fails.

charts.title: VlogReward
charts.note: The explicit rubric and stronger comparison reward improve both ranking accuracy and the ability to tell editors what to change next, because the model now receives supervision about which dimension failed and how far apart competing edits are.

items.b: Subjective dimensions can still be noisy.
items.html: Even with a rubric, creators may disagree on what counts as creativity or ideal pacing, so labels can contain real ambiguity that limits reward-model consistency.

items.b: The rubric may miss niche creator goals.
items.html: A fixed six-dimensional taxonomy can underspecify styles that rely on unusual editing choices or domain-specific narrative conventions.

items.b: Feedback quality depends on comparison coverage.
items.html: If the training set does not include enough high-quality and low-quality variants for similar footage, inter-group ranking becomes less informative and the reward model can lose calibration.
The method is strongest when the dataset spans diverse creator styles and the downstream system uses the full score profile rather than collapsing the result back to one number.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take one set of raw vlog clips and produce several candidate edit plans with controlled differences: some should damage pacing by cutting too fast or too slowly, some should break narrative consistency by scrambling shot order, and some should improve shot quality while keeping the story intact. Run a baseline judge that outputs only one score and run VlogReward on the same candidates.

The demo should show two things. First, VlogReward should rank the best edits more reliably because it can compare across richer quality differences. Second, its dimension-level scores should identify the exact failure mode in each weak candidate, allowing a simple refinement loop to fix one dimension at a time.
demo.closing: A convincing demo is one where overall rank improves and refinement_gain is positive for the dimensions the feedback targeted, because that shows the reward model is useful for editing rather than only for passive evaluation.
